items.title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Maco-RL tackles the challenges of scaling mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) by introducing a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts and a Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) mechanism. The scheduler stabilizes training by balancing gradient contributions, while TBS efficiently allocates compute to samples based on mastery, promoting exploration and preserving learned skills. This approach enables a unified policy to continually expand its capabilities across multiple domains without needing separate specialists or distillation.
items.figure_caption: Our Maco-RL enables 27B-sized models to substantially outperform baselines and even be competitive with much larger models in terms of overall pass rates across multiple task domains, i.e., issue- and feature-oriented coding, terminal and Claw. Experimental results reveal that Maco-RL more effectively turns compute budget into model capability. (a) Average pass rates over five benchmarks, i.e., Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Claw-Anything, Tests Passed on FeatureBench 1.1 and Pass 3 \( \mathrm{Pass}^{3} \) on Claw-Eval, against model sizes, which are P total ​ P active \( \sqrt \){P_{\( \mathrm{total} \)}P_{\( \mathrm{active} \)}} for MoE models and P total P_{\( \mathrm{total} \)} otherwise. (b) The mean Pass@1 metrics against compute budget for RL on mixed and single tasks. For single-task RL, we sum compute across the three tasks.

items.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces REE, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the scientific research capabilities of AI agents. REE presents 100 open-ended research problems, sourced from active scientific fields and reviewed by experts, requiring agents to iteratively improve a starter solution within a time limit. The core contribution is a standardized evaluation method that scores agent performance against expert solutions, providing a quantitative measure of their ability to advance scientific understanding.
items.figure_caption: An REE task in four steps. (1) The agent receives a problem statement, a starter solution, development data, and an offline environment with a checker. (2) It improves the solution iteratively for up to 12 hours, and its saved versions are evaluated at five checkpoints. (3) One grader evaluates the starter solution, the agent’s solution, and the expert solution on the same held-out test instances. (4) Each metric value is mapped to a score from 0, the starter solution, to 100, the upper bound of the metric. The margin M = B − E M=B-E compares the agent’s score B B with the expert baseline E E .

items.title: VisualMontage: Manipulating the Beliefs of Vision-Language Agents with Authentic Image Sequences
items.abstract: This paper introduces VisualMontage, a framework for simulating "visual cognitive collusion" attacks on vision-language models (VLMs). The core method involves using authentic image sequences with locally faithful captions to trick VLMs into inferring attacker-chosen claims through their own reasoning. The main contribution is a new benchmark and a systematic evaluation of this threat, demonstrating how coordinated visual and textual content can manipulate VLM beliefs.
items.figure_caption: Comparison of multimodal attack strategies. Image-centric attacks fabricate or alter visual content, while channel-centric attacks convey hidden signals or malicious payloads. Our cognitive-centric attack instead combines authentic images to manipulate the victim VLM’s beliefs through self-induced misleading relations inferred across otherwise faithful posts.

items.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
items.abstract: This paper introduces DFly2, a method to accelerate speculative decoding for long-context language models. DFly2 leverages the inherent sparsity of the target model's attention mechanism to efficiently share its context cache and attention selections with the draft model. This significantly reduces memory usage and prefill time, while improving decode concurrency by avoiding redundant computations.

items.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces CARE-OPD, an adaptive on-policy distillation method for long-horizon agents. It addresses limitations in existing prefix replay by strategically collecting teacher trajectories seeded by student actions to ensure broader history coverage, and by using response-level confidence gating to filter unreliable updates. Furthermore, it employs hindsight replay allocation to prioritize reusing critical trajectory segments, making the distillation process more efficient and effective.
items.figure_caption: Overview of CARE-OPD. Left: Factorization of prefix replay in agent OPD (above). Method overview (below). Right: The plots compare SWE-bench Verified task success, end-to-end time, and environment actions on Qwen3.5 family. The bottom panel reports mean collection trajectory length on SWE and Deep Research. Async OPD denotes online asynchronous one-turn distillation, and Prefix Replay denotes vanilla prefix replay.

items.title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
items.abstract: DemoFoundry addresses the challenge of acquiring realistic robot training data by using coding agents to generate photorealistic, physically grounded demonstrations. The core method involves agents creating aligned real-proxy video pairs to train a renderer and then writing interaction programs to generate new synthetic data. This approach overcomes the visual gap in simulation and the action alignment issues in video-only generation, enabling scalable robot learning without requiring human demonstrations for new tasks.

items.title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach where Large Language Models (LLMs) directly synthesize control policies by reading and reasoning over world models (environment source code). This method bypasses traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, achieving comparable or superior performance with significantly less experience. The core contribution is demonstrating that LLMs can translate environmental knowledge into interpretable, executable decision rules, effectively replacing the need for extensive RL interaction.
items.figure_caption: Comparison of conventional RL and policy synthesis from readable world models.

items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.abstract: DRBench Pro introduces a novel knowledge-centric evaluation for deep research agents, focusing on the breadth and depth of research directions covered. Its core method involves building knowledge trees from Wikipedia and generating queries and rubrics based on these trees, allowing for structured assessment of information synthesis. The contribution is a benchmark that precisely measures how well agents explore complex topics by evaluating their coverage of major research directions and related knowledge chains.
items.figure_caption: Structured knowledge coverage in DRBench Pro. (a) Reports with the same flat coverage can exhibit different coverage patterns over a shared reference tree. (b) Overview of five native search LLMs’ performance on DRBench Pro.

items.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
items.abstract: This paper introduces Delta Residue Attribution (DRA) to analyze unneeded edits in coding agent patches. DRA traces edits to their origin, reverts them, and reruns tests to determine necessity. The study finds that while agents make more edits, a significant portion are for tests and documentation, and their core code edits are often as necessary as human developers'.

items.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
items.abstract: PersonaFactory addresses the limitation of LLMs generating stylistically flat synthetic user prompts. It creates a large bank of detailed user personas with diverse backgrounds and communication styles. These personas are then used to augment existing prompts, generating a vast corpus of persona-styled conversations across many languages, improving LLM training data for better persona control.

items.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
items.abstract: This paper addresses memory hallucinations in LLM agents, where retrieved external memories are ignored or misapplied. The authors propose TASK memory, a novel approach that combines textual memory with activation steering and knowledge editing. This method aims to resolve conflicts between parametric knowledge and external memory, thereby reducing hallucinations and improving the agent's ability to accurately utilize recalled information.
items.figure_caption: Memory hallucination: the memory is correct, the answer is not. (a) Text-only memory or RAG puts the retrieved note into the prompt and leaves the rest to the frozen model, where the note in the context conflicts with the stale fact in the weights. On a question about the memory, the weights win and the model answers with the stale fact (Type I, memory-ignoring). On a question about another entity, the note wins and the model assigns the memory to the wrong entity (Type II, memory-misapplying). Across our five models these rates reach 46% and 24%, and Type II reaches 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing. (b) TASK memory goes beyond text-only memory. Each memory object holds T ext content, a K nowledge edit Δ ​ W m \( \Delta \) W_{m} whose key u ^ m \( \hat{u}_{m} \) serves as the in-model address, and a pair of A ctivation- S teering vectors ( v + , v − ) (v^{+},v^{-}) that carry no content. For a query x x , the address response r m ​ ( x ) r_{m}(x) is compared with the threshold \( \tau_{m} \) . A relevant query shows T , loads E and adds v + v^{+} , so the model adopts the memory; an unrelated query leaves T and E off and adds v − v^{-} , so the model keeps its own answer.

items.title: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context
items.abstract: This paper investigates the value of mathematical theories for LLM solvers. It demonstrates that providing the correct theory significantly improves problem-solving accuracy and efficiency for LLMs, outperforming worked examples. The research also explores LLMs' ability to induce theories and quantifies how much of the benefit from an oracle theory can be recovered through this induction process.

items.title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
items.abstract: ZeroHero trains small language agents (SLAs) from scratch by first pre-training them to mimic a large language model expert's responses on successful trajectories. Subsequently, these SLAs are fine-tuned using PPO with an added "reasoning alignment" objective that supervises their generated language alongside environmental rewards. This method enables the creation of capable, specialized language agents with significantly reduced model capacity.
items.figure_caption: ZeroHero agents use language to reason, search, and ask questions across three interactive environments.

items.title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
items.abstract: VulnSafe introduces Vulnerability-Aware Response Competence (VARC) to measure a LLM's ability to provide emotionally supportive interactions. VARC assesses five relational safety constructs, evaluated through 2,050 prompts across 41 scenarios. This benchmark offers a more nuanced understanding of LLM safety beyond isolated violations, distinguishing between proactive and prohibitive behaviors.
items.figure_caption: An illustrative capability contrast. The left response displays surface empathy but encourages exclusive reliance on the system. The right response recognizes the relational risk, maintains an appropriate boundary, and supports connection to real-world resources.

items.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces $μ$-Bench, a novel benchmark for evaluating multi-user voice agents in shared environments. It simulates interdependent user requests, considering individual goals, privacy, and task constraints within a closed-loop system. The core contribution is a comprehensive evaluation framework that measures joint task success and identifies failure causes, revealing significant performance gaps in current voice agents.
items.figure_caption: Overview of \( \mu \) -Bench: multi-user task coordination and domain coverage. Left (Top): A shared full-duplex voice agent handles overlapping speech, barge-ins, peer side-talk, and backchannels while invoking backend tools. Left (Bottom): The same trajectory is diagnosed along Attribution (routing actionable speech), Threading (retaining and updating active goals), and Coordination (reconciling constraints and authority), with success requiring all goals and constraints to hold jointly. Right: Distribution of 100 base scenarios across 20 domains, split between 51 Tool-Augmented (408 cases) and 49 Tool-Free (392 cases) scenarios; parentheses show TA/TF counts.

items.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
items.abstract: This paper surveys the security, privacy, and ethical challenges of using Large Language Models (LLMs) in telecommunications. It introduces a novel taxonomy that connects LLM risks to specific telecom use cases and sensitive data characteristics. The contribution lies in identifying and categorizing these unique challenges, highlighting open research areas like longitudinal data privacy and scalable guardrails for responsible LLM deployment in the telecom sector.

items.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
items.abstract: This paper reveals that AI monitor evaluations can be misleading due to the attack policies used. The false negative rate of a monitor is highly sensitive to how attack policies are generated and optimized, leading to potentially false confidence in a monitor's strength if only basic attacks are used. The study demonstrates that even optimized attacks against proxy monitors can effectively transfer to a held-out target monitor.

items.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
items.abstract: This paper introduces Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a method to generate more effective training data for hard math problems. DART tackles the scarcity of correct reasoning traces by decomposing incorrect ones, identifying uncertain steps, and then generating diverse, alternative paths to the correct solution. This approach significantly improves the ability of LLMs to solve challenging math problems compared to standard sampling methods.
items.figure_caption: DART decomposes a rejected trace into self-contained reasoning steps ( Section 2.1 ), selects a non-final reasoning step based on its position-weighted uncertainty ( Section 2.2 ), proposes a deliberately distinct alternative candidate ( Section 2.3 ), and then greedily decodes a new continuation. This procedure can be repeated for a fixed number of iterations or until a target number of accepted traces is obtained.

items.title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering
items.abstract: This paper introduces Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent (KBGD) for self-structuring learning in knowledge base construction. KBGD iteratively refines a knowledge base's structure by proposing edits that minimize discrepancies between expected and actual answers. Its core contribution is a gradient-descent-like approach that learns to optimize the knowledge base's organization based on question-answering performance, enabling more effective information retrieval for LLM applications.

items.title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
items.abstract: RePace is an offline framework that reasons about how much to accelerate each part of a human demonstration for vision-language-action (VLA) policies. It evaluates candidate speedup factors by measuring sequence shortening and comparing the resulting training data quality. This allows for faster VLA policies without needing a separate speed-selection module at deployment.
items.figure_caption: Offline demonstration acceleration with RePace . RePace compares how candidate speedup factors change the observations and action targets used for VLA fine-tuning. It uses the recorded scene and motion to interpret these changes and select a speedup profile.

arxiv.title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
arxiv.abstract: RePace is an offline framework that reasons about how much to accelerate each part of a human demonstration for vision-language-action (VLA) policies. It evaluates candidate speedup factors by measuring sequence shortening and comparing the resulting training data quality. This allows for faster VLA policies without needing a separate speed-selection module at deployment.
arxiv.figure_caption: Offline demonstration acceleration with RePace . RePace compares how candidate speedup factors change the observations and action targets used for VLA fine-tuning. It uses the recorded scene and motion to interpret these changes and select a speedup profile.

papers.title: Maco-RL: Scaling Agent Capabilities with Mixed-Task Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Maco-RL tackles the challenges of scaling mixed-task reinforcement learning (MixRL) by introducing a quota-based scheduler for asynchronous rollouts and a Tri-Buffer Sampling (TBS) mechanism. The scheduler stabilizes training by balancing gradient contributions, while TBS efficiently allocates compute to samples based on mastery, promoting exploration and preserving learned skills. This approach enables a unified policy to continually expand its capabilities across multiple domains without needing separate specialists or distillation.
papers.figure_caption: Our Maco-RL enables 27B-sized models to substantially outperform baselines and even be competitive with much larger models in terms of overall pass rates across multiple task domains, i.e., issue- and feature-oriented coding, terminal and Claw. Experimental results reveal that Maco-RL more effectively turns compute budget into model capability. (a) Average pass rates over five benchmarks, i.e., Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Claw-Anything, Tests Passed on FeatureBench 1.1 and Pass 3 \( \mathrm{Pass}^{3} \) on Claw-Eval, against model sizes, which are P total ​ P active \( \sqrt \){P_{\( \mathrm{total} \)}P_{\( \mathrm{active} \)}} for MoE models and P total P_{\( \mathrm{total} \)} otherwise. (b) The mean Pass@1 metrics against compute budget for RL on mixed and single tasks. For single-task RL, we sum compute across the three tasks.

papers.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces REE, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the scientific research capabilities of AI agents. REE presents 100 open-ended research problems, sourced from active scientific fields and reviewed by experts, requiring agents to iteratively improve a starter solution within a time limit. The core contribution is a standardized evaluation method that scores agent performance against expert solutions, providing a quantitative measure of their ability to advance scientific understanding.
papers.figure_caption: An REE task in four steps. (1) The agent receives a problem statement, a starter solution, development data, and an offline environment with a checker. (2) It improves the solution iteratively for up to 12 hours, and its saved versions are evaluated at five checkpoints. (3) One grader evaluates the starter solution, the agent’s solution, and the expert solution on the same held-out test instances. (4) Each metric value is mapped to a score from 0, the starter solution, to 100, the upper bound of the metric. The margin M = B − E M=B-E compares the agent’s score B B with the expert baseline E E .

papers.title: VisualMontage: Manipulating the Beliefs of Vision-Language Agents with Authentic Image Sequences
papers.abstract: This paper introduces VisualMontage, a framework for simulating "visual cognitive collusion" attacks on vision-language models (VLMs). The core method involves using authentic image sequences with locally faithful captions to trick VLMs into inferring attacker-chosen claims through their own reasoning. The main contribution is a new benchmark and a systematic evaluation of this threat, demonstrating how coordinated visual and textual content can manipulate VLM beliefs.
papers.figure_caption: Comparison of multimodal attack strategies. Image-centric attacks fabricate or alter visual content, while channel-centric attacks convey hidden signals or malicious payloads. Our cognitive-centric attack instead combines authentic images to manipulate the victim VLM’s beliefs through self-induced misleading relations inferred across otherwise faithful posts.

papers.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
papers.abstract: This paper introduces DFly2, a method to accelerate speculative decoding for long-context language models. DFly2 leverages the inherent sparsity of the target model's attention mechanism to efficiently share its context cache and attention selections with the draft model. This significantly reduces memory usage and prefill time, while improving decode concurrency by avoiding redundant computations.

papers.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces CARE-OPD, an adaptive on-policy distillation method for long-horizon agents. It addresses limitations in existing prefix replay by strategically collecting teacher trajectories seeded by student actions to ensure broader history coverage, and by using response-level confidence gating to filter unreliable updates. Furthermore, it employs hindsight replay allocation to prioritize reusing critical trajectory segments, making the distillation process more efficient and effective.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of CARE-OPD. Left: Factorization of prefix replay in agent OPD (above). Method overview (below). Right: The plots compare SWE-bench Verified task success, end-to-end time, and environment actions on Qwen3.5 family. The bottom panel reports mean collection trajectory length on SWE and Deep Research. Async OPD denotes online asynchronous one-turn distillation, and Prefix Replay denotes vanilla prefix replay.

papers.title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
papers.abstract: DemoFoundry addresses the challenge of acquiring realistic robot training data by using coding agents to generate photorealistic, physically grounded demonstrations. The core method involves agents creating aligned real-proxy video pairs to train a renderer and then writing interaction programs to generate new synthetic data. This approach overcomes the visual gap in simulation and the action alignment issues in video-only generation, enabling scalable robot learning without requiring human demonstrations for new tasks.

papers.title: Do We Still Need Reinforcement Learning When We Can Read the World Model?
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach where Large Language Models (LLMs) directly synthesize control policies by reading and reasoning over world models (environment source code). This method bypasses traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, achieving comparable or superior performance with significantly less experience. The core contribution is demonstrating that LLMs can translate environmental knowledge into interpretable, executable decision rules, effectively replacing the need for extensive RL interaction.
papers.figure_caption: Comparison of conventional RL and policy synthesis from readable world models.

papers.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
papers.abstract: DRBench Pro introduces a novel knowledge-centric evaluation for deep research agents, focusing on the breadth and depth of research directions covered. Its core method involves building knowledge trees from Wikipedia and generating queries and rubrics based on these trees, allowing for structured assessment of information synthesis. The contribution is a benchmark that precisely measures how well agents explore complex topics by evaluating their coverage of major research directions and related knowledge chains.
papers.figure_caption: Structured knowledge coverage in DRBench Pro. (a) Reports with the same flat coverage can exhibit different coverage patterns over a shared reference tree. (b) Overview of five native search LLMs’ performance on DRBench Pro.

papers.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Delta Residue Attribution (DRA) to analyze unneeded edits in coding agent patches. DRA traces edits to their origin, reverts them, and reruns tests to determine necessity. The study finds that while agents make more edits, a significant portion are for tests and documentation, and their core code edits are often as necessary as human developers'.

papers.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
papers.abstract: PersonaFactory addresses the limitation of LLMs generating stylistically flat synthetic user prompts. It creates a large bank of detailed user personas with diverse backgrounds and communication styles. These personas are then used to augment existing prompts, generating a vast corpus of persona-styled conversations across many languages, improving LLM training data for better persona control.

papers.title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination
papers.abstract: This paper addresses memory hallucinations in LLM agents, where retrieved external memories are ignored or misapplied. The authors propose TASK memory, a novel approach that combines textual memory with activation steering and knowledge editing. This method aims to resolve conflicts between parametric knowledge and external memory, thereby reducing hallucinations and improving the agent's ability to accurately utilize recalled information.
papers.figure_caption: Memory hallucination: the memory is correct, the answer is not. (a) Text-only memory or RAG puts the retrieved note into the prompt and leaves the rest to the frozen model, where the note in the context conflicts with the stale fact in the weights. On a question about the memory, the weights win and the model answers with the stale fact (Type I, memory-ignoring). On a question about another entity, the note wins and the model assigns the memory to the wrong entity (Type II, memory-misapplying). Across our five models these rates reach 46% and 24%, and Type II reaches 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing. (b) TASK memory goes beyond text-only memory. Each memory object holds T ext content, a K nowledge edit Δ ​ W m \( \Delta \) W_{m} whose key u ^ m \( \hat{u}_{m} \) serves as the in-model address, and a pair of A ctivation- S teering vectors ( v + , v − ) (v^{+},v^{-}) that carry no content. For a query x x , the address response r m ​ ( x ) r_{m}(x) is compared with the threshold \( \tau_{m} \) . A relevant query shows T , loads E and adds v + v^{+} , so the model adopts the memory; an unrelated query leaves T and E off and adds v − v^{-} , so the model keeps its own answer.

papers.title: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the value of mathematical theories for LLM solvers. It demonstrates that providing the correct theory significantly improves problem-solving accuracy and efficiency for LLMs, outperforming worked examples. The research also explores LLMs' ability to induce theories and quantifies how much of the benefit from an oracle theory can be recovered through this induction process.

papers.title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
papers.abstract: ZeroHero trains small language agents (SLAs) from scratch by first pre-training them to mimic a large language model expert's responses on successful trajectories. Subsequently, these SLAs are fine-tuned using PPO with an added "reasoning alignment" objective that supervises their generated language alongside environmental rewards. This method enables the creation of capable, specialized language agents with significantly reduced model capacity.
papers.figure_caption: ZeroHero agents use language to reason, search, and ask questions across three interactive environments.

papers.title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: VulnSafe introduces Vulnerability-Aware Response Competence (VARC) to measure a LLM's ability to provide emotionally supportive interactions. VARC assesses five relational safety constructs, evaluated through 2,050 prompts across 41 scenarios. This benchmark offers a more nuanced understanding of LLM safety beyond isolated violations, distinguishing between proactive and prohibitive behaviors.
papers.figure_caption: An illustrative capability contrast. The left response displays surface empathy but encourages exclusive reliance on the system. The right response recognizes the relational risk, maintains an appropriate boundary, and supports connection to real-world resources.

papers.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces $μ$-Bench, a novel benchmark for evaluating multi-user voice agents in shared environments. It simulates interdependent user requests, considering individual goals, privacy, and task constraints within a closed-loop system. The core contribution is a comprehensive evaluation framework that measures joint task success and identifies failure causes, revealing significant performance gaps in current voice agents.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of \( \mu \) -Bench: multi-user task coordination and domain coverage. Left (Top): A shared full-duplex voice agent handles overlapping speech, barge-ins, peer side-talk, and backchannels while invoking backend tools. Left (Bottom): The same trajectory is diagnosed along Attribution (routing actionable speech), Threading (retaining and updating active goals), and Coordination (reconciling constraints and authority), with success requiring all goals and constraints to hold jointly. Right: Distribution of 100 base scenarios across 20 domains, split between 51 Tool-Augmented (408 cases) and 49 Tool-Free (392 cases) scenarios; parentheses show TA/TF counts.

papers.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
papers.abstract: This paper surveys the security, privacy, and ethical challenges of using Large Language Models (LLMs) in telecommunications. It introduces a novel taxonomy that connects LLM risks to specific telecom use cases and sensitive data characteristics. The contribution lies in identifying and categorizing these unique challenges, highlighting open research areas like longitudinal data privacy and scalable guardrails for responsible LLM deployment in the telecom sector.

papers.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
papers.abstract: This paper reveals that AI monitor evaluations can be misleading due to the attack policies used. The false negative rate of a monitor is highly sensitive to how attack policies are generated and optimized, leading to potentially false confidence in a monitor's strength if only basic attacks are used. The study demonstrates that even optimized attacks against proxy monitors can effectively transfer to a held-out target monitor.

papers.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a method to generate more effective training data for hard math problems. DART tackles the scarcity of correct reasoning traces by decomposing incorrect ones, identifying uncertain steps, and then generating diverse, alternative paths to the correct solution. This approach significantly improves the ability of LLMs to solve challenging math problems compared to standard sampling methods.
papers.figure_caption: DART decomposes a rejected trace into self-contained reasoning steps ( Section 2.1 ), selects a non-final reasoning step based on its position-weighted uncertainty ( Section 2.2 ), proposes a deliberately distinct alternative candidate ( Section 2.3 ), and then greedily decodes a new continuation. This procedure can be repeated for a fixed number of iterations or until a target number of accepted traces is obtained.

papers.title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent (KBGD) for self-structuring learning in knowledge base construction. KBGD iteratively refines a knowledge base's structure by proposing edits that minimize discrepancies between expected and actual answers. Its core contribution is a gradient-descent-like approach that learns to optimize the knowledge base's organization based on question-answering performance, enabling more effective information retrieval for LLM applications.

It evaluates candidate speedup factors by measuring sequence shortening and comparing the resulting training data quality. This allows for faster VLA policies without needing a separate speed-selection module at deployment.
